title: 기본 모음 (Basic Vowels)
description: Learn the 10 fundamental vertical and horizontal vowels: ㅏ, ㅑ, ㅓ, ㅕ, ㅗ, ㅛ, ㅜ, ㅠ, ㅡ, ㅣ.
explanation: Korean vowels are built using three elements: • (heaven), ㅡ (earth), and ㅣ (man).
Vertical vowels (ㅏ, ㅑ, ㅓ, ㅕ, ㅣ) have their long stroke standing up. Horizontal vowels (ㅗ, ㅛ, ㅜ, ㅠ, ㅡ) have their long stroke lying flat.
Adding a short stroke adds a 'y' sound: ㅏ (ah) becomes 야 (yah).
takeaway: Vowels cannot stand alone in writing; they use a silent 'ㅇ' placeholder if no consonant is present.

practice.prompt: Write the syllable block for the sound 'ah' (using the silent placeholder)

title: 기본 자음 (Basic Consonants)
description: Learn the first set of simple consonants: ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅅ, ㅇ, ㅈ, ㅎ.
explanation: Korean letters are written inside imaginary squares, moving from left to right and top to bottom.
Consonants change slightly depending on the vowel: ㄱ sounds like a soft 'g/k', ㄴ is 'n', ㄷ is 'd/t', and ㄹ is a flapped 'r/l' sound.
ㅅ is an 's' sound, but it turns into a soft 'sh' sound when paired with ㅣ or 'y' vowels (like ㅑ, ㅕ, ㅛ, ㅠ).
takeaway: Consonants sit to the left of vertical vowels, or on top of horizontal vowels.

title: 이중 모음 (Double Vowels)
description: Master complex combined vowel sounds like ㅐ, ㅔ, ㅘ, ㅝ, ㅟ, ㅢ.
explanation: Double vowels are created by smashing two vowels together.
ㅐ (ae) and ㅔ (e) sound almost identical in modern spoken Korean. Don't worry about distinguishing them by ear—focus on spelling.
Combination rules: ㅗ blends with ㅏ (ㅘ = wa). ㅜ blends with ㅓ (ㅝ = wo). ㅢ (ui) is unique: it sounds like 'ee' when combined with consonants.
takeaway: Think of combination vowels as gliding sounds (w + vowel).

title: 격음 & 경음 (Aspirated & Double Consonants)
description: Understand strong and tense consonants: ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ, ㅊ and ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅆ, ㅉ.
explanation: Aspirated consonants (ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ, ㅊ) are pronounced with a strong puff of air. Hold a hand before your mouth; you should feel a burst of breath.
Double consonants (ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅆ, ㅉ) are tense. Tighten your vocal cords and release the sound firmly with no air bursting out.
takeaway: Tense consonants have a higher pitch than their basic counterparts.

title: 받침: 기본 (Basic Final Consonants)
description: How single consonants sit at the bottom of a block and change sound.
explanation: Consonants at the very bottom of a block are called 받침 (Batchim).
While there are many consonants, they only make 7 final sounds when resting at the bottom: ㅂ/ㅍ sound like [P], ㄱ/ㅋ/ㄲ sound like [K], and ㄴ, ㅁ, ㅇ, ㄹ retain their core values.
Crucially, ㄷ, ㅌ, ㅅ, ㅆ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅎ all flatten into a blunt [T] sound at the end of a syllable if no vowel follows.
takeaway: Batchim sounds are unreleased—stop the air instantly at the end of the syllable.

title: 겹받침 (Double Final Consonants)
description: Master complex double batchim combinations like ㄺ, ㄻ, ㄼ, ㄶ.
explanation: Some Korean syllable blocks carry two different consonants in the final position.
Rule 1: If the word stands alone, you usually pronounce only one of the letters. For example, in 닭 (chicken), the ㄹ is silent, leaving you with [dak].
Rule 2 (Linking): If the next block begins with the placeholder ㅇ, the second consonant rolls over to blend into the next vowel: 닭이 is read as [달기] (dal-gi).
takeaway: Double batchim look scary but follow logical phonetic conversion systems.

practice.prompt: Spell the word for 'chicken' (dak - uses 'ㄺ' batchim)
Spell the base verb 'to sit' (an-tta - uses 'ㄵ' batchim + 다)
Spell the native number for 'eight' (yeo-deol - uses 'ㄼ' batchim)
